extracted.intended_audience: astronomical photographers and observers preparing over-exposed corona/transit plates (late-19th-century wet-collodion technique)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and experimental criteria for producing and diagnosing irradiation (halation) in over-exposed astronomical plates (corona / transit photography), and methods to avoid or reduce those artefacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographic irradiation (inner and outer fringes) — recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: In all over-exposed photographs of luminous objects upon a dark background, the brighter parts of the picture are found to be surrounded by a nebulous haze or border of light ... divided into two parts—an inner and very marked border of light, following the contour of the luminous objects, and an outer and much less definite haze.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize two distinct components when diagnosing over-exposed plates: an inner, sharply marked border (inner fringe) that fades gradually outward and an outer, fainter haze (outer halo). Note that the true image boundary is difficult to locate because the inner border fades from the image outward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outer haze cause — reflections from back of the plate
rubrics_metrics.description: From these experiments we may conclude that the outer haze is produced by reflections from the back of the plate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: on ebonite (opaque) plates the outer haze disappeared; on yellow glass it was fainter; wet black paper backing greatly reduced it; grinding and black varnish on back rendered outer haze imperceptible. Use these observations to attribute an observed outer halo to back-surface reflections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding outer halo — use opaque plates or black-backed transparent plates
rubrics_metrics.description: The outer irradiation halo may therefore be entirely avoided for the future in any corona or other necessarily over-exposed photographs by the use of the opaque plates... If it is considered important that the negatives should be capable of being copied by transmitted light, the outer halo may still be to a great extent avoided by the use of transparent glass plates with a backing of wet black paper or black varnish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational choices: (a) use opaque (e.g., ebonite) plates when transmitted-light copying is unnecessary; (b) when transmitted-light copying is needed, back transparent plates with wet black paper or black varnish (or grind/back-coat) to greatly reduce outer halo. Explanation: reducing refractive-index change at glass/film interface reduces back reflections; light then absorbed by black backing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner irradiation edge cause — optical imperfections (not collodion chemistry)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is clearly proved that the inner irradiation edge is not caused by any chemical or other action taking place within the thickness of the collodion; but must be referred to the optical imperfections of the instrument which throws the image upon the collodion film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose inner fringe as instrument/optical origin (aberrations, circles of least diffusion) rather than chemical action in the collodion. Expect the inner fringe to remain even after eliminating back reflections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental test to distinguish collodion action vs optical cause (ivory-ruler test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place an ivory ruler with a bevelled edge in immediate contact with the collodion film and expose so that the image falls partly on the collodion and partly on the ivory; if the scene of action lay within the collodion film, the inner irradiation fringe might extend under the edge of the ruler; if due to optical imperfections, the image would be cut off sharply by the edge of the ruler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure details: keep ruler in place, briefly expose to gas-burner light to faintly print the ruler edge on collodion before development. Interpreting result: a sharp cutoff at ruler edge indicates optical cause; faint action under ruler attributable to imperfect opacity of ivory or capillary film effects. Use this controlled contact test to localize the locus of irradiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capillary-film/collodion swelling observation and artefact explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: A very narrow bright line appears, which indicates the presence of a small capillary film of liquid along the edges of the ruler, forming a minute cylindricallens... we may therefore conclude that the collodion film is slightly swelled or thickened by the action of the light upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting contact-test results, account for small bright lines and slight convexity of image ends as due to capillary films and slight swelling/thickening of collodion under illumination rather than chemical encroachment of the image. Be cautious attributing minute encroachments to chemistry without ruling out these optical/mechanical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chromatic aberration tests — limited effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A bath of solution of sulphate of copper was placed ... forming a blue screen ... seemed to have very little effect in altering the breadth of the irradiation-fringe, only slightly retarding the rate of its formation; a similar result was obtained on placing a piece of yellow glass ... formation of the fringe was still further retarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using blue or yellow screening/filters produced only slight retardation of fringe formation, indicating chromatic aberration is not the primary cause of the inner fringe. Therefore, chromatic correction alone may not eliminate the inner irradiation edge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation of inner fringe by stopping lens edges (avoid oblique pencils)
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers have long known that by making use of stops they can obtain a much sharper image. ... we cut off the edges of the lens with a circular stop, and found that the inner irradiation-fringe was thus greatly decreased. It seems, therefore, fair to argue that the aberration of oblique pencils exceeds in magnitude the other disturbing causes, and that it will be well ... to avoid as much as possible all oblique pencils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical remedy: use aperture stops (cut off lens edges) to reduce aberration from oblique pencils; in preparing for solar/corona photography, minimize oblique rays to reduce inner fringe. This supports instrument/stop design choices as key to image sharpness under over-exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plate placement and instrument selection — put plates in primary focus; reflectors favored
rubrics_metrics.description: We would, therefore, place our photographic plates in the primary focus, and thus avoid the necessarily deep curves of any arrangement of lenses which may be used for enlarging the image. Whether it would be best to make use of a reflector or a refractor, remains to be settled by further experiment, but our present experiences would lead us to vote in favour of the reflector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: mount plates at the primary focus to avoid additional lens-group curvature and oblique-pencil aberrations introduced by enlarging optics; consider using reflectors (less chromatic aberration / different oblique-behaviour) based on present tests, though further experiments are advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of irradiation on exposure time and relative brightness
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been found to vary with the time of exposure, and the relative brightness of the object and its background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning exposures for luminous objects on dark backgrounds, expect irradiation extent to increase with exposure time and with higher brightness contrast. Use exposure control as part of strategy to manage irradiation alongside optical and backing measures.
